name: Clontarf Castle — Gothic Revival country house, rebuilt 1836–37
address: Clontarf Castle Hotel, Castle Avenue, Clontarf, Dublin 3
historical_description: Detached country house rebuilt in 1836–37, comprising a square-plan tower-house form with curved corners and a taller rear tower, attached to a complex-plan Gothic Revival house with gabled bays, porch and canted bay windows. NIAH records carved limestone copings and finials, crenellated parapets, octagonal chimneystacks, carved door surrounds and extensive surviving interior features including plasterwork ceilings, timber wainscoting and joinery, fireplaces and encaustic tiled floors. historical_significance: The present castle is the 1836–37 Gothic Revival rebuilding commissioned by J.E.V. Vernon and designed by William Vitruvius Morrison. It deliberately uses medieval architectural references and varied tower forms to evoke a building developed over centuries. The NIAH appraisal identifies its carved stonework and surviving interior craftsmanship as significant.

name: Warrenpoint gate lodge — 84 Clontarf Road

historical_description: Detached two-bay single-storey former gate lodge, built circa 1840, with an entrance loggia on the east-facing front. NIAH records a hipped natural slate roof, red-brick chimneystacks with cornices and clay pots, carved fascia boards with cusping, cast-iron rainwater goods, lined-and-ruled rendered walls, label-moulded window openings and paired three-pane round-headed timber casements. The entrance is set within a group of red-brick gate piers, a segmental arch and masonry sphinx finials, with smooth rendered quadrant walls.
historical_significance: NIAH identifies this as one of the earliest buildings to develop on the Clontarf seafront, predating the associated terrace of six houses to the north-east. name: 86 Clontarf Road

historical_description: Terraced two-bay, two-storey house over a raised basement, built in 1847, with a two-storey return to the rear. The round-headed entrance has a petal-motif fanlight, a corniced and friezed door surround supported by console brackets, and a timber-panelled door. Cut-granite entrance steps and platform retain a cast-iron balustrade; the property is set back behind cast-iron railings on a cut-granite plinth and a pedestrian gate. historical_significance: NIAH identifies the house as part of a substantial terrace built in 1847 by Isaac Warren, steward of the Vernon estate, on land obtained from that estate. Historic fabric survives particularly at the entrance platform, door surround and railings.

name: Church of St John the Baptist — Seafield Road West

historical_description: Cruciform-plan Church of Ireland church built 1864–1866, with porch and vestry added 1897–1899. name: Kilmainham Mill — former flour and textile mill complex
address: Kilmainham Lane / Rowserstown Lane, Kilmainham, Dublin 8
historical_period: c.1815–1825; expanded in the mid-to-late 19th century
historical_description: A surviving early nineteenth-century industrial mill complex beside the River Camac. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage records an attached L-plan, four-storey former flour mill built c.1820, with a two-storey brick extension and later concrete extension. Dublin City Council's September 2023 project briefing records a mid-to-late nineteenth-century expansion that included a steam engine, a rerouted headrace serving a new water wheel, a cast-iron sectional aqueduct and cast-iron internal columns. The mill later changed from flour and corn processing to cloth finishing around 1903/04; industrial activity ceased in 2000. This record covers the surviving mill complex, not the medieval predecessor mill: the earlier water-powered activity is evidenced historically but is not catalogued here as a separately located surviving structure.
historical_significance: A rare surviving example of Dublin's early nineteenth-century milling and textile-finishing industry, retaining evidence of successive power and production systems beside the River Camac. Dublin City Council described it in 2023 as the last remaining largely unaltered early nineteenth-century flour mill in Dublin and probably the last remaining fulling mill in Ireland.
access_status: The complex is owned by Dublin City Council. DCC's September 2023 briefing states that accessibility was limited and facilities for widespread use were not available at that time. Do not enter the site, buildings or work areas without explicit permission. Confirm current public access and photography permission with Dublin City Council before any visit; photograph only from lawful public viewpoints.

name: Dublin United Tramway Company Powerhouse (Windmill Lane Recording Studios) — RPS 7381
address: 20 Ringsend Road, Dublin 4, D04 CF66
historical_description: A surviving Art Deco former electrical power station built for the Dublin United Tramways Company. Specialist architectural history identifies Vincent Kelly as architect and dates the building to 1932. The current occupier confirms that No. 20 Ringsend Road was once the electrical power station for the tramline depot and that the recording studios have occupied the building since 1990. Dublin City Council's current Record of Protected Structures lists RPS 7381 as the Ringsend Shelbourne Pierrot Club (former Bovril building), described as a commercial warehouse/sound studio. The sources indicate a layered industrial and cultural history: tramway electricity generation, later Bovril-associated use, and recording-studio use. The exact chronology of the intermediate Bovril phase requires further archival confirmation.
historical_significance: A surviving physical link to Dublin's electric tramway infrastructure and a notable Art Deco industrial building later adapted for music recording. It also illustrates the reuse of former industrial buildings in the Docklands. The current recording-studio use gives the building a continuing cultural role, but private interiors are not part of public access.
access_status: Private recording-studio premises. Exterior may be viewed from the public footpath; do not enter or photograph internal studio spaces without arranging permission. The studio offers a separately booked visitor tour; check its current terms before any interior visit.

historical_description: The red lighthouse at the seaward end of the Great South Wall, marking the entrance to Dublin Port. Dublin Port records that the light was first lit on 29 September 1767, replacing a floating light previously used to warn shipping. The Dictionary of Irish Architects records John Smyth's responsibility for the lighthouse's construction in 1766–1767 and the eastern abutment of the South Wall in or after 1771. The exact chronology of later alterations is not fully established by the sources reviewed for this record.
historical_significance: A landmark piece of Dublin's maritime navigation and harbour-engineering infrastructure, physically associated with the Great South Wall and the historic entrance to the port.
national_inventory_reference: Dublin City Council RPS 6798 — Great South Wall (to lighthouse); the cited register entry covers the wall and does not constitute a separate lighthouse entry.
access_status: The lighthouse stands at the seaward end of the Great South Wall. The breakwater is exposed to wind, waves and changing weather; check current access notices, closures and port restrictions before fieldwork. Do not enter operational or restricted port areas. The evidence reviewed here does not establish unrestricted access to the Pigeon House precinct.

The source-derived point is the depicted-object coordinate, not the photographer's camera location. The wider Great South Wall and Pigeon House precinct contain several separately protected and archaeologically recorded assets; these are retained as research leads pending current survival, exact geometry, access and photographic verification.

name: Former Pigeon House Hotel (Teach Pigeon) — late-Georgian harbour hotel
address: Pigeon House Road, Poolbeg Peninsula, Dublin 4
historical_description: Classical dressed-ashlar granite building of three storeys over basement, with full-height bows at either end of the south-east elevation and entrance facing the Liffey and its harbour. Construction commenced in 1793 and was completed in 1795; design attributed to Robert Pool. Built for cross-channel passengers, it became part of the historic Pigeon House defence precinct in 1798 and remained within the precinct until 1897. The 3FM EIAR records it as standing. The Film Office lists short-term office/location use; March 2026 reporting describes rooms used by a wastewater operator under a council letting proposal, whose final terms are not established here.
historical_significance: Rare surviving late-eighteenth-century harbour hotel associated with passenger travel and the later Pigeon House precinct.
access_status: Not a public visitor attraction. Photograph only from a lawful public viewpoint or with express permission; do not enter the building or grounds.

name: Half Moon Battery (Five Gun Battery) — surviving coastal-defence fabric and swimming-club site
address: Great South Wall, Poolbeg Peninsula, Dublin 4
historical_description: The Board of Ordnance constructed a gun battery on the Great South Wall in 1793, approximately 800m from Poolbeg Lighthouse, to control the river channel and waters around the lighthouse. The 3FM EIAR catalogue describes it as armed with five 24-pounder guns, subsequently dismantled, with part of the structure surviving. The south-facing perimeter wall is granite-built and is the most intact upstanding element; a curvature in the Great South Wall surface is believed to mark a former gun swivel position. The present site includes the Half Moon swimming-place and club buildings. A separate Dublin Port Heritage Conservation Strategy describes the battery as a three-gun platform, so the historical gun-count requires source reconciliation.
historical_significance: Surviving coastal-defence fabric associated with the late-eighteenth-century protection of Dublin Bay and the approach to the Liffey.
access_status: The site is associated with an active swimming club and Great South Wall. Do not enter club buildings or restricted areas without permission; photograph only from lawful public access and respect swimmers and club operations.

name: Former Pigeon House Lifeboat House — archaeological site with surviving wall stubs (DCIHR 19-09-008)
address: Great South Wall, near Poolbeg Lighthouse, Dublin 4
historical_period: c.1850; lifeboat presence at Pigeon House recorded as early as 1815
historical_description: The 3FM EIAR catalogue identifies the Lifeboat House as a site, not a complete standing building. It records a lifeboat at Pigeon House as early as 1815, although it was apparently later transferred to Bullock. For the c.1850 lifeboat-house site, only lengths of ruined wall stubs remain above ground; surviving fabric includes red brick and granite. An enclosure wall of old concrete construction also survives, breached in places, and the perimeter path is ruinous from coastal processes. A historical photograph from 1939 in Dublin Port Archives shows standing remains at the station site.
historical_significance: Physical and documentary evidence of nineteenth-century lifeboat provision and maritime rescue infrastructure at the entrance to Dublin Port.
access_status: The EIAR describes ruinous wall stubs, breached enclosure wall and a derelict perimeter path affected by coastal processes. Do not climb or cross unstable remains; verify safe lawful access and stay clear of port-restricted land.

name: Sluice House, South Wall — former Rathmines and Pembroke drainage control building (DCIHR 19-09-009-01)
address: Great South Wall, Poolbeg Peninsula, Dublin 4
historical_description: Detached three-bay, single-storey masonry former sluice house built around 1881 in association with Londonbridge Road Pumping Station and the Rathmines and Pembroke Main Drainage Scheme. The 3FM EIAR describes squared-random rubble stone walls with concrete coping and rusticated quoins; segmental-headed window openings with rusticated block-and-start surrounds, now blocked; and a square-headed doorway with rusticated granite surround and a steel door installed around 1990. The building housed machinery operating two penstock valves to manage sewage flow and seawater pressure at the sewer outlet. It is now described as abandoned, retaining much of its original form and stonework.
historical_significance: A surviving example of late-nineteenth-century municipal drainage engineering, associated with Ireland's first completed main sewerage scheme.
access_status: Described as abandoned in the EIAR. Confirm lawful public access and present condition before visiting; do not enter the building or fenced/operational utility land.

name: Masonry landing slip at eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort (DCIHR 19-09-012)
address: Great South Wall beside the eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort, Dublin 4
historical_description: A substantial masonry boat slip adjoining the Great South Wall beside the eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort. The 3FM EIAR catalogue records it as constructed around 1770 and shown on both the Ordnance Survey First Edition 6-inch series and 25-inch maps. It measures approximately 25m long and 4.3m wide, slopes gently west-to-east at about 10 degrees, and has a surface of rectangular granite masonry similar to the facing blocks of the adjacent Great South Wall. The report records it standing up to 1.6m above the foreshore, with four courses of granite masonry visible; sheet piles protrude from silty sand on the channel side.
historical_significance: A rare, individually documented eighteenth-century maritime landing structure contemporary with the construction of the Great South Wall.
access_status: The slip is at the eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort within a port landscape with access restrictions. The EIAR also notes sheet piles and foreshore conditions. Do not approach from unstable foreshore or enter restricted land; photograph only from a lawful, safe public viewpoint or with permission.

The stonework comprises long rectangular masonry blocks, approximately 1m to 1.3m long, laid at right angles to the sea wall. name: Magazine Fort — eighteenth-century military powder magazine
address: St Thomas Hill, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_period: 1734–1736; modified c.1760 and 1801; conservation and phased reopening 2023–2026
historical_description: Freestanding, broadly square-plan military magazine fort with four demi-bastions, watch-towers, an eastern extension and ranges of barrack and magazine buildings. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage dates the complex to 1730–1810 and describes its principal construction phases around 1735, c.1760 and 1801. It was designed as a powder magazine for Dublin and retains original magazine chambers and evidence of successive military uses. The Office of Public Works led a major conservation programme; the fort reopened for guided public tours in 2026.
historical_significance: A nationally rated military complex associated with the defence and supply infrastructure of Dublin and the 1916 Rising. Its conservation and 2026 reopening make it an especially important current heritage site.
access_status: The fort reopened for guided public tours in 2026. Access is by booked guided tour; check the Phoenix Park Visitor Centre / OPW booking information before travelling. Do not enter outside authorised visitor routes or conservation areas.

name: Wellington Monument (Wellington Testimonial)
address: South-eastern Phoenix Park, near Islandbridge Gate, Dublin 8
historical_description: Freestanding granite obelisk, 62 metres tall, designed by Sir Robert Smirke as a testimonial to Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington. The monument stands on a three-stepped monumental pedestal and a square-plan stylobate. Four bronze plaques cast from cannons captured at Waterloo are set into its faces; three carry bas-reliefs and the eastern face bears a Latin and English inscription. The monument is also known as the Wellington Testimonial.
historical_significance: A nationally rated monumental work and one of the defining nineteenth-century features of Phoenix Park. Its bronze plaques, relief sculpture and inscriptions make it a multi-part visual and epigraphic subject.
access_status: Located in Phoenix Park. Photograph from public paths and safe viewpoints; respect any temporary barriers, events or maintenance closures. Do not cross fences or approach unsafe slopes.

name: Ashtown Castle — restored fortified tower house
address: Phoenix Park Visitor Centre, Chesterfield Avenue, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_period: c.1605; later incorporated into Ashtown Lodge c.1760; restored in the 1990s
historical_description: Detached three-storey fortified tower house with a square-plan stair tower to the south-east, built around 1605. The building has uncoursed limestone rubble walls, a pitched slate saddle-back roof behind parapets, a dressed-stone chimney, small square-headed windows and defensive loops. It was incorporated into a larger Georgian residence around 1760; that later lodge was subsequently demolished. The tower was restored and now forms part of the Phoenix Park Visitor Centre heritage experience.
historical_significance: A rare surviving fortified house of the early seventeenth century close to Dublin city, preserving evidence of the earlier Ashtown demesne and later park administration.
access_status: The castle is within the Phoenix Park Visitor Centre area. Check current visitor-centre opening hours and any guided-tour or exhibition restrictions before visiting. Photograph only from permitted public areas.

name: The Phoenix Monument — Portland-stone Corinthian column and phoenix
address: Central roundabout, Chesterfield Avenue, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_description: Freestanding Portland-stone Corinthian column erected in 1747 and surmounted by a carved stone phoenix rising from the ashes. The full-height fluted shaft has a Corinthian capital and stands on a plinth with inscribed marble plaques to the east and west and carved coats of arms to the north and south. Its stepped granite base is enclosed within a circular platform of stone setts. The monument stands at the central junction of Chesterfield Avenue, Acres Road and Odd Lamp Road.
historical_significance: One of the earliest surviving features of Phoenix Park and a focal point on its principal avenue. The column, phoenix sculpture, plaques, heraldry and surrounding stone-sett platform each merit separate visual documentation.
access_status: The monument occupies the centre of a road junction/roundabout. Do not enter the carriageway or traffic island. Photograph only from safe public paths and viewpoints.

name: Park Gate — Phoenix Park's historic limestone entrance
address: Park Gate, Chesterfield Avenue, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_description: Principal entrance gateway at the city end of Chesterfield Avenue, comprising two pairs of round-plan ashlar limestone vehicular piers with moulded plinths and cornices, gadrooned caps and electrified wrought-metal and glass lanterns. Rebuilt square-headed pedestrian entrances flank the vehicular openings. The adjoining park wall is ashlar limestone over a rubble-stone plinth. The gate piers were dismantled in 1932 to facilitate the Eucharistic Congress and re-erected in 1986.
historical_significance: A prominent entrance ensemble within the historic designed landscape of Phoenix Park, combining stone carving, metalwork, lighting and boundary-wall construction.
access_status: Public park entrance and adjoining public realm. Photograph from footpaths and safe pedestrian viewpoints; keep clear of traffic and do not obstruct the entrance.

The Office of Public Works describes the reinstatement as a key part of the fort's conservation and phased reopening.

name: Papal Cross — 1979 papal mass steel monument
address: Fifteen Acres, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_description: Freestanding steel cross erected in 1979 on a granite-flagged platform atop a grass-covered mound approached by a flight of thirty-three granite-flagged steps. Designed by Ronnie Tallon of Scott Tallon Walker for the outdoor Papal Mass celebrated by Pope John Paul II during his first and only pastoral visit to Ireland. name: Knockmaree burial monument — surviving Neolithic cist
address: Knockmaree / Knockmary, west of St Mary's Hospital, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_period: Late Neolithic burial mound with later Early Bronze Age burials; excavated in the nineteenth century
historical_description: A Linkardstown-type burial monument recorded as National Monument Service record DU018-00711. The Phoenix Park Conservation Management Plan describes a cemetery mound originally about 40 metres wide and up to 3 metres high. Excavation revealed a central cist formed by five upright stones supporting a large capstone; the cist is the only element of the original mound recorded as surviving. The central burial included at least three male inhumations and grave goods including a shell necklace, bone toggle and flint blade. Four small Early Bronze Age cists containing cremated remains and food vessels were also recorded. The exact age and sequence should be expressed using the archaeological report's period terms rather than an unsupported single calendar date.
historical_significance: A rare surviving prehistoric funerary structure within Phoenix Park, documenting Neolithic and Early Bronze Age burial practices and the long archaeological history of the park landscape.

name: George's Dock — Georgian wet dock and lock entrances

name: Loop Line Railway Viaduct — Beresford Place and Liffey crossing
address: Beresford Place, Gardiner Street Lower and River Liffey, Dublin 1
historical_description: Thirteen-span railway viaduct built around 1891 to carry the City of Dublin Junction Railway across Beresford Place and the River Liffey, connecting Connolly Station with the line to Dún Laoghaire. The NIAH describes four stylistically distinct components: a three-span steel girder bridge over Gardiner Street Lower with riveted decorative parapet panels and cylindrical columns; a two-span masonry arch section with yellow-brick voussoirs and rusticated limestone spandrels; a five-span steel girder section over Beresford Place with lattice parapets and granite piers; and a three-span Liffey crossing with fish-belly girders supported on cast-iron caissons. The Beresford Place piers include Portland-stone classical detailing.
historical_significance: A major work of late-Victorian railway engineering by John Challoner Smith, built by Arroll Brothers of Glasgow. It connected the Dublin and Wicklow railway route with Amiens Street (Connolly) Station and supported the Royal Mail route. Its combination of steel, masonry, granite, Portland stone and cast-iron caissons makes it an unusually rich subject for architectural and engineering documentation.

name: Sheriff Street Lifting Bridge — Spencer Dock bascule bridge

historical_description: Single-span bascule bridge installed over Spencer Dock between 1939 and 1941. The NIAH records that it is now fixed and retains a pair of reclaimed cut-limestone panels with rope-twist detailing and the date “1873”, carrying the emblem of the Midland Great Western Railway of Ireland. name: Westmoreland, Buckingham and Camden Sea Locks — Grand Canal Dock entrance
address: North-east entrance of Grand Canal Dock at the River Liffey, Dublin 2
historical_description: Group of three sea locks built in 1796 to connect Grand Canal Dock with the tidal River Liffey. The NIAH records tooled-granite walls and coping on the central dock platforms, inscriptions recording names and dates, machinery notches and lock-gate emplacements, cast-iron ladders and rings, three sets of double-leaf timber gates with timber beams and some later metal panels, stone setts and limestone paving, and winch mechanisms on the eastern and central platforms. historical_description: Attached triple-gable-fronted former malt house built around 1890, comprising three single-storey blocks with attics. The NIAH records pitched roofs, moulded yellow-brick eaves cornice, carved granite coping, brown-brick front elevation with granite quoins and plinth, rubble-limestone walling, pattress plates, triple lancet windows with carved block-and-start surrounds and granite sills, infilled openings and segmental-headed doorways.
historical_significance: Part of the industrial group around Grand Canal Docks. The three gabled fronts, carved granite details and surviving industrial fabric form a distinctive architectural composition, built around the time the neighbouring sugar refinery was converted to a distillery.

name: Grand Canal Quay — Guinness former malt house of 1886
address: Grand Canal Quay, Dublin 2
historical_description: Attached twenty-one-bay, four-storey former malt house built by the Guinness brewery in 1886, with three attic bays and later continuous glazed attic extension. The NIAH records Flemish-bond yellow brick above snecked limestone ground-floor walls, granite stringcourses and quoins, cast-iron rainwater goods, pattress plates, square- and segmental-headed openings, brick reveals and granite sills. Remodelled in 1995 by T.J. Cullen and Co. The skewed end accommodates the adjacent railway line.
historical_significance: A substantial surviving component of the Guinness industrial landscape at Grand Canal Dock, illustrating the close relationship between brewing, canal transport and rail freight. The brick-over-limestone construction and unusual skewed end are key architectural features.

name: Hanover Quay — 1790 limestone dockside quay
address: Hanover Quay, north side of Grand Canal Dock, Dublin 2
historical_description: Quayside built around 1790 along the north side of Grand Canal Docks. historical_significance: An individually registered surviving edge of the 1796 Grand Canal Dock, retaining late-eighteenth-century limestone construction and cast-iron mooring fittings. name: Pumphouse No. 1 — Alexandra Basin Heritage Zone
address: Alexandra Road, Dublin Port, Dublin 1
historical_period: c.1910; southern section added shortly afterwards
historical_description: Detached gable-ended brick pumphouse built around 1910 beside the southeast corner of the former Graving Dock. historical_significance: A surviving component of Dublin's nineteenth- and twentieth-century ship-repair infrastructure and an important remnant of the former graving-dock precinct. name: Redbrick Electricity Substation — East Wall Road / Alexandra Road
address: Corner of East Wall Road and Alexandra Road, Dublin 1
historical_description: Detached corner-sited two-storey electricity substation built around 1900. The NIAH describes a single-bay breakfronted west elevation and three-bay north elevation, flat roof concealed behind a brick parapet with moulded granite coping, red brick in Flemish bond, moulded brick string course and cornice, gauged round-headed window openings, granite sills and an arched entrance framed by brick Doric piers. Dublin Port states that the building played a pivotal role in the early electrification of the Port. It has been restored and adapted as a museum, with a new largely glazed extension.
historical_significance: A surviving piece of early electrical infrastructure associated with the modernisation of Dublin Port. Its carefully detailed brickwork gives an otherwise utilitarian service building architectural significance. Refurbishment also exposed part of the earlier 1728 sea wall beneath the building; that buried wall is a separate archaeological feature and is not treated as visible fabric of the substation.

name: Dublin Port Diving Bell — Stoney's compressed-air quay-construction caisson
address: Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_period: Designed mid-nineteenth century; delivered 1866; entered service 1871; fabricated c.1870; used until 1958
historical_description: Cast-iron and riveted plate-iron diving bell designed by Dublin Port engineer Bindon Blood Stoney and built by Grendon and Company of Drogheda. The NIAH describes a chamber approximately 23 feet square by 6.5 feet high, accessed by a vertical shaft with iron rungs and incorporating an air lock. The bell was lowered from a floating platform so workers could excavate and level the riverbed under compressed air before large precast concrete quay-wall blocks were placed. It was moved to Sir John Rogerson's Quay in 1989 and is mounted on a modern display structure.
historical_significance: An exceptionally important surviving artefact of nineteenth-century harbour engineering and compressed-air construction. Dublin Port's archive records its role in building the North Wall Extension and Alexandra Basin; the bell is now part of Dublin Port's Distributed Museum and a publicly accessible interpretive installation.

name: 2 Sir John Rogerson's Quay — former Tedcastle Steamer Company warehouse (Bushell Ltd. Furniture)
address: 2 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_description: Attached gable-fronted three-bay, two-storey former warehouse built in 1913–14. NIAH records a pitched slate roof set perpendicular to the street with a glazed clerestory, carved granite coping to the gable, cast-iron rainwater goods, red-brick Flemish-bond walls, granite string courses and red-brick pilasters with granite coping. The front elevation includes recessed brick panels, blocked segmental-headed ground-floor openings, square-headed upper windows with bull-nosed brick surrounds and an oculus at the gable apex. A double-height round-headed opening with raised brick pilasters was added around 1980. NIAH identifies its former name as Tedcastle Steamer Company and describes later occupation by the British & Irish Steam Packet Company.
historical_significance: A regional-rated mercantile warehouse illustrating the early-twentieth-century commercial and maritime character of Sir John Rogerson's Quay. NIAH attributes the design to James Evans for ship-owner Tedcastle McCormack. The façade is separately listed by Dublin City Council as protected structure RPS 7543.

name: Dublin Tropical Fruit Company warehouse — Tropical Fruit Warehouse
address: 30–32 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_period: c.1890; established as Tropical Fruit Company warehouse in 1892; restored and redeveloped 2019–2022
historical_description: Attached double-gable-fronted fourteen-bay two-storey former warehouse built c.1890 for the Dublin Tropical Fruit Company, with its use for tropical-fruit imports recorded from 1892. The NIAH describes an M-profile pitched slate roof set perpendicular to the street with clerestory, terracotta ridge tiles, red-brick Dutch gables with decorative terracotta apex tiles, carved limestone cornice, brick pilasters, limestone string courses, coping and orb finials, Flemish-bond brickwork, polychrome and cogged brick string courses, segmental-headed openings and carved limestone keystones. The historic warehouse was later restored and integrated with a substantial modern office redevelopment, including elevated glazed office floors and a new building to the rear. The historic warehouse fabric must be distinguished from these later additions.
historical_significance: A prominent surviving late-Victorian docklands warehouse and a rare physical record of Dublin's tropical-fruit import trade. Its façade also preserves two earlier riverine keystones associated with Carlisle Bridge and sculptor Edward Smyth. The building's layered history includes the Hibernian Marine School site, the Tropical Fruit Company, later U2 management offices and contemporary adaptive reuse; these phases are documented by different sources and should not be conflated.

name: Anna Liffey riverine keystone — salvaged Carlisle Bridge carving
address: Set into the street-facing façade of the Tropical Fruit Warehouse, 30–32 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2; west-side riverine keystone
historical_period: Sculpted 1794; originally associated with Carlisle Bridge; later incorporated into the Tropical Fruit Company warehouse façade, relocation date not established
historical_description: One of two original riverine figurehead keystones incorporated into the façade of the former Tropical Fruit Company warehouse. NIAH identifies the west-side head as Anna Liffey and states that the riverine keystones were sculpted by Edward Smyth in 1794 for Carlisle Bridge. When Carlisle Bridge was reconstructed as O'Connell Bridge in 1880, the original keystones were too large for the altered arches; smaller replicas were made, and the originals later found their way to the warehouse façade. The precise date and circumstances of their relocation are not established by the sources consulted.
historical_significance: An individually significant surviving piece of eighteenth-century Dublin sculpture, retaining an original carved river-god keystone from the predecessor of O'Connell Bridge. It connects the history of the Liffey crossing, the work of sculptor Edward Smyth and the later maritime warehouse on Sir John Rogerson's Quay.

name: British & Irish Steam Packet Company offices — The Shipping Office protected structure
address: 20–24 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, at the junction with Lime Street, Dublin 2
historical_period: Built 1909; formally opened 1910; integrated into The Shipping Office redevelopment completed 2025
historical_description: Freestanding six-bay, two-storey former shipping-company offices with attic storey, built in 1909, with integral carriage arches to the end bays, shallow projections to the north frontage, a west wing wall and a triple-pile goods shed to the rear. NIAH records pitched slate roofs with terracotta ridge cresting, red-brick chimneystacks, a red-brick parapet with carved masonry capping, clerestories to the rear store roofs, Flemish-bond brickwork, carved limestone details, round-headed ground-floor windows, oculi, elliptical-headed carriage arches with terracotta keystones, cast-iron wheel stops, a loading platform and cobbled yard. The company moved its offices here in 1909 and the building was formally opened in 1910. The historic structure has since been integrated into the modern mixed-use development known as The Shipping Office; the modern glazed atrium and new office development are later additions and must not be mistaken for the 1909 building.
historical_significance: A surviving protected shipping-office building associated with the British & Irish Steam Packet Company, a major Irish Sea shipping operator established in Dublin in 1836. The building records the commercial and operational history of the port through its offices, carriage arches, rear goods sheds and loading infrastructure. Its classically influenced brick-and-stone façade was designed by W.H. Byrne & Sons. The historic structure now forms part of a contemporary redevelopment, illustrating adaptive reuse of a docklands industrial-era building.

name: The Ferryman — former pair of Georgian houses, 35–36 Sir John Rogerson's Quay
address: 35–36 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, at Cardiff Lane, Dublin 2
historical_description: Corner-sited attached former pair of three-bay, four-storey houses, built c.1820 and now used as a public house and guest house. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage records an M-profile hipped slate roof, red-brick chimneystacks, red-brick parapet with granite coping, Flemish-bond brick walls, square- and round-headed window openings, granite sills, surviving timber sliding-sash windows, and round-headed door openings with carved Portland-stone architrave and marigold lintel carvings. The two houses were originally separate. NIAH records Michael Scanlon and James Lynch as occupants in the 1850s; contemporary trade directories listed a grocer and shipbuilder at No. 35 and a ship smith at No. 36.
historical_significance: A rare surviving early nineteenth-century quay-side pair that preserves the scale, materials and commercial character of the historic Sir John Rogerson's Quay streetscape. Its carved stone doorcase, timber sash windows and diminishing fenestration are notable architectural details. The site also records the former mix of domestic, retail and maritime trades along the quay.

historical_description: Attached gable-fronted five-bay, three-storey former mill built c.1890, now recorded by NIAH as offices. name: Great South Wall — registered historic sea wall and breakwater
address: Linear maritime monument extending from the Dodder estuary / Ringsend towards Poolbeg Lighthouse, Dublin Bay; not represented by a single point coordinate
historical_period: 1715–1795, with multiple construction phases and later alterations
historical_description: The Great South Wall is a long, phased maritime engineering structure associated with the development of Dublin Port. The 3FM heritage report describes the piled works initiated in the early eighteenth century, the Ballast Office Wall completed in 1759, and the later masonry extension towards Poolbeg and the lighthouse. The Great South Wall is identified in the report as a registered archaeological monument and protected structure. Its component sections differ in construction and present visibility; parts are buried, missing above ground, or remain visible as wall and parapet sections.
historical_significance: A major eighteenth-century engineering work that shaped the navigation channel and Dublin's relationship with Dublin Bay. Its surviving and buried sections preserve evidence of harbour engineering, coastal protection, port development and successive construction methods.
national_inventory_reference: RMP DU018-066 and DU019-029; Dublin City Council RPS 6928 (as cited in the 3FM report)
access_status: The wall is a long linear monument crossing public, port-owned, industrial and restricted areas. Public access varies by segment and may change. Do not assume the full route or every surviving wall section is accessible.
photography_restrictions: Do not enter port or ESB lands, industrial sites, fenced compounds, the cooling-water outfall or restricted areas. Photograph only from lawful public viewpoints and obey all barriers, signs and site rules. Never climb the wall or approach exposed water edges in unsafe conditions.
photography_brief: Photograph only clearly accessible sections from public paths
Record each segment's visible condition and distinguish original historic fabric from later boundary walls
Capture changes in wall alignment, parapet height and masonry material without touching the structure
Record missing or buried stretches as such rather than inferring exact subsurface geometry
Use founder GPS only at a safe public standing point and record the precise photographed feature separately from the linear parent site
research_notes: This is a linear-site parent record and deliberately has no point coordinate or single WALK THERE destination. The 3FM heritage report identifies RMP DU018-066 and DU019-029 and RPS 6928 for the Great South Wall. Exact segment geometry, condition and access must be assessed separately. Do not conflate the Ballast Office Wall (1759) with the later granite-faced Great South Wall extension towards Poolbeg.
